rashi:a1.1: Mishna. From sanctity to sanctity: items consecrated for Temple maintenance that one consecrated for the altar, he has done nothing. And with items consecrated for the altar, one does not alter them from the sanctity of a burnt offering to a peace offering, or from a peace offering to a burnt offering.
rashi:a1.2: And one may consecrate them: this refers to items consecrated for the altar.
rashi:a1.3: A consecration of value: for example, if he said of a burnt offering, “This is hereby for Temple maintenance,” it is appraised in money according to the share he has in it, and he gives [that sum] to the treasurer. As we learned in Arakhin, in the chapter HaMakdish (Arakhin 28b): A person may dedicate his consecrated items; if it was a vow, he gives their value, and if it was a gift-offering, he gives their benefit. That is to say: if this animal was a vow, for example he said, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering,” and set this one aside for his vow, then since he bears responsibility for it if it dies or is stolen, it turns out that it is wholly his, and he gives its entire value to the priest’s dedication. And the same holds for Temple maintenance, if he associated items consecrated for the altar with Temple maintenance. And if it was a gift-offering, then since he bears no responsibility for it if it dies, it turns out that he has no share in it except the benefit of discretion: he is allowed to take a small sum from a fellow Israelite in exchange for giving this burnt offering of his to [the Israelite’s] daughter’s son, a priest, to sacrifice it, so that he may take the hide. And according to that benefit of discretion he gives to Temple maintenance.
rashi:a1.4: And one may dedicate them: if he dedicated items consecrated for the altar, he gives the priest the value, as I explained.
rashi:a1.5: If they died: items consecrated for the altar, even after they became blemished, but were not yet redeemed, are buried; he cannot redeem them and feed them to the dogs. And even according to the one who says that one may redeem consecrated animals to feed them to the dogs, that applies when they became tereifa, where standing and valuation is still possible; but if they died, not, since we require standing and valuation. Alternatively, this “died” is, for example, where he transgressed and slaughtered them before their redemption, and it says that he can no longer redeem them and eat them, since we require standing and valuation; and they are buried.
rashi:a1.6: They can be redeemed: because they were not included in [the halakha of] standing and valuation, as the reason is shown in the Gemara.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Hekdesh ilui is a term of appraisal, like “they raise it in money”: one assesses how much of a share he has in the animal, as Arakhin (28b) explains of one who associates a burnt offering with Temple maintenance: if it was a vow he gives its value, since had it been lost he would have had to pay; if a gift-offering, he gives according to the benefit of discretion in it. Rashi explains that benefit as a small sum a fellow Israelite would pay to have it offered in the watch of his daughter’s son, a priest. Tosafot object that this expression is found only regarding the firstborn (Bekhorot 27a), and prefer what Arakhin teaches explicitly: with a gift-offering, one assesses how much a person would want to give for this ox to offer it as a burnt offering, even though he is not “permitted,” meaning not obligated (as “craftsmen are not permitted to stand,” Ḥullin 54b). Arakhin derives the consecration of value from “every dedicated item is most holy”: a dedication takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and on offerings of lesser sanctity. The consecration of value refers to items consecrated for the altar, since the Gemara says that items consecrated for Temple maintenance associated with the altar or with the priests’ dedications are nothing. Rashi’s reason there, that the benefit of discretion does not apply to them, did not satisfy Tosafot’s teacher, since one could ask of them too how much a person would want to give; rather, with items consecrated for the altar the owner has a standing to redeem them once they become blemished, while with items he consecrated for Temple maintenance he has no more claim than anyone else, so it is not in his power to associate them. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. Dedications to priests: these are unspecified dedications. And he used the expression “dedications to priests” because sometimes dedications are for Temple maintenance, for example if he specified and said, “This is hereby a dedication for Temple maintenance.”
rashi:a2.2: He has done nothing: and he does not give the priests even the consecration of value.
rashi:a2.3: Every dedicated item that is most holy: that was holy to the Lord from the outset, belongs to the Lord, and the priest’s claim does not take effect on it.
tosafot:a2.1: Every dedicated item is most holy unto the Lord: at first glance, Rav Huna holds like the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in tractate Arakhin, chapter HaMakdish (Arakhin 28b). There Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says: unspecified dedications are for Temple maintenance, as it is stated, “Every dedicated item is most holy unto the Lord.” And the Rabbis say: unspecified dedications are for the priests; then what does the verse teach by “every dedicated item is most holy”? It teaches that a dedication takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and on offerings of lesser sanctity. According to that tanna [the Rabbis], Rav Huna’s interpretation works well, since what he says, that it teaches that it takes effect on consecrated items, refers specifically to dedications that are “to the Lord.” But according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira one cannot interpret it this way, since [for him the verse] does not speak of association by a consecration of value at all. [So writes] HaRaMaR.
gershom:a1.1: One may not alter them from one sanctity to another: and not even from a lighter sanctity to a more stringent sanctity, for example from a peace offering to a burnt offering.
gershom:a2.1: And one may consecrate them: meaning, items consecrated for the altar.
gershom:a3.1: A consecration of value: for the sake of items consecrated for Temple maintenance, and that value he gives to Temple maintenance. And what is the value? As we say in Arakhin, in the chapter HaMakdish Sadehu: if it was a vow, that he said, “This ox is incumbent upon me as a burnt offering,” he bears responsibility for it, since he cannot avoid sacrificing it; and since he bears responsibility for it, he gives its value to Temple maintenance, since he consecrated it with a consecration of value for Temple maintenance. And if that item consecrated for the altar which he consecrated for its value was a gift-offering, where he did not say “incumbent upon me” but “This is hereby a burnt offering,” so that he does not bear responsibility for it, he gives to Temple maintenance only the value of its benefit. And what is its benefit? One assesses how much another priest, who is not of the watch serving at that time, would want to give the owner of the ox for this ox, so that he wait for him until the time of his watch and give it to him to offer as a burnt offering, so that he may acquire its hide; for this priest is not permitted to offer it except in the time of his watch. And as much as that priest would want to give him, that is what he gives to Temple maintenance; and this is the value.
gershom:a4.1: And one may dedicate them: items consecrated for the altar; he may say, “Let them be a dedication.” And if so, if they are a vow, he gives their value to the priests, and if a gift-offering, he gives its benefit, as we said.
gershom:a5.1: Items consecrated for the altar that one associated with dedications to priests, saying, “Let them be a dedication”: he has said nothing, and he gives the priests neither their value nor their benefit.
gershom:a6.1: As the verse states: “Every dedicated item is most holy unto the Lord.” This implies that every dedication that comes from items consecrated for the altar, if he dedicated it, shall be to the Lord and not to the priests, because he cannot associate them, since they are not his; therefore he has done nothing. And it infers from the precise wording of the baraita: but items consecrated for the altar that one associated with dedications to priests take effect for the value, as I said, and he gives it to the priests. A refutation of Rav Huna.
rashi:a3.1: He has done nothing: because their body is not removed from Temple maintenance, and the benefit of discretion does not apply to them.
tosafot:a3.1: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance that one associated, whether with items consecrated for the altar or with dedications to priests, he has done nothing: Rashi explained: granted, items consecrated for the altar have a benefit of discretion, as is explained in the mishna; but with items consecrated for Temple maintenance, what benefit of discretion is there in them?
rashi:a4.1: And similarly dedications to priests: he has no share in them at all, not even the benefit of discretion, because he may give them only to a priest of that [serving] watch; and [this is] according to the one who compares movable property to dedications of land, in Arakhin, in the chapter HaMakdish (Arakhin 28a).
tosafot:a4.1: Dedications to priests that one associated, etc.: Rashi explained that he has no benefit of discretion in them, since he must give it to the priest of that watch; “and even according to the one who does not compare movable property to land, that applies to one who consecrates” — end of his words. [Our printed Rashi reads “according to the one who compares.”] And my teacher says: this matter of comparing movable property to land is in Arakhin, chapter HaMakdish (Arakhin 28a): Rav Ḥisda said: one who dedicates movable property gives it to any priest he wishes, as it is stated, “Every dedicated item in Israel shall be yours”; if he dedicated his fields, he gives them to the priest of that watch. And it asks: but let us compare movable property to land! And it answers: is it not a dispute of tanna’im, since there is one who compares and one who does not? As for what he explained, “even according to the one who does not compare, that applies to one who consecrates,” my teacher did not understand his wording. Rather, my teacher thinks it should be explained as a case where he was a priest, and here it follows the one who does not compare.
rashi:a5.1: But items consecrated for the altar: to which the benefit of discretion applies, what he did is done, and he gives the benefit of discretion to the priest.
rashi:a6.1: That he omitted it: items consecrated for the altar, which he did not teach together with these.
rashi:a6.2: He omitted it on account of this one: that is, on account of this matter he omitted it: if he consecrated them for Temple maintenance, what he did is done and he gives a consecration of value; but for dedications to priests, not, because the verse explicitly excluded it.
gershom:a7.1: Rav Huna could say to you: when he omitted the inference, not teaching it in the baraita, he omitted it for this inference: but items consecrated for the altar that one associated for their value with items consecrated for Temple maintenance take effect. But he did not mean the inference you drew, for dedications to priests, since for dedications to priests they do not take effect, as I said. If so, since they do not take effect for dedications to priests, let him teach it explicitly in the baraita alongside those of which it teaches “he has done nothing.”
rashi:a7.1: Let him teach it alongside these: and say, “Items consecrated for the altar that one associated with dedications to priests, he has done nothing.”
rashi:a7.2: Two: that one cannot associate them even with one of the two sanctities.
gershom:a8.1: It teaches those in which there are two: for example, “whether with items consecrated for the altar or with items consecrated for Temple maintenance, he has done nothing.” But this case, items consecrated for the altar that one associated with dedications to priests, in which there are not two, it does not teach: for with dedications to priests they do not take effect, but with items consecrated for Temple maintenance they do take effect. Therefore it does not teach it in the baraita.
gershom:a9.1: Another version: it teaches [the cases] that can be taught with two; and this amounts to the same thing.
rashi:a8.1: Is it not a consecration of value: one consecrates it for Temple maintenance; and “one dedicates” that it teaches is for dedications to priests, and he gives the priests the value.
gershom:a10.1: Is it not a consecration of value for the sake of items consecrated for Temple maintenance, and he gives their value to Temple maintenance; and “one dedicates them,” and he gives their value to the priests’ dedications?
rashi:a9.1: There is no difference when he expresses: items consecrated for the altar [that he gives] to Temple maintenance, whether in a term of consecration or in a term of dedication, he gives the value to the treasurers.
gershom:a11.1: No, both this and that: “and one dedicates them” also speaks of the needs of Temple maintenance. And it says that there is no difference whether he expresses items consecrated for the altar in a term of consecration, or says, “Let them be a dedication for Temple maintenance”: they take effect for Temple maintenance, for the value.
gershom:a12.1: But it is not taught so in the baraita, as you answer, for it teaches explicitly “and one dedicates them: dedications to priests,” meaning to the priests. And isn’t it taught, etc.
gershom:a13.1: But Rav Huna states a verse: for he said, “Every dedicated item is most holy; it shall be to the Lord,” meaning, and not to the priests.
rashi:a11.1: Ulla said: the verse does not read like Rav Huna. It implies: since it could have written “A dedicated item is most holy,” and it writes “and every dedicated item,” it implies this: a dedication takes effect on everything, even on something that is most holy.
gershom:a14.1: Ulla said: the verse comes for this: “dedicated item, every dedicated item.” Since it could have said “dedicated item,” what is “every dedicated item”? It teaches that a dedication takes effect on every single sacred item, whether on offerings of the most sacred order, which are the Lord’s, or on offerings of lesser sanctity, for the value, as we said.
gershom:a15.1: And did Ulla say this: that a dedication takes effect on items consecrated for the altar?
tosafot:a12.1: In brief: Rashi explains “only the delay of the treasurers” to mean the offering is not sacrificed until the treasurers come to stand over it (as “how can a person’s offering be sacrificed while he does not stand over it?”), but no monetary value goes to Temple maintenance, and all the more so not to the priests’ dedications, since even Rav Huna, who disputes regarding the priests’ dedications, agrees regarding Temple maintenance. And the answer “by rabbinic law” means that the earlier baraita, which omitted items consecrated for the altar so as to say a consecration of value takes effect on them, speaks of rabbinic law, since by Torah law there is only the treasurers’ delay; Ulla too answered by rabbinic law, the verse is mere support, and its main point is to include dedications in misuse, since it says of them “to the Lord.” Tosafot find this very difficult: (1) the mishna itself says “one may consecrate them by a consecration of value”; (2) Arakhin (28b) derives from “every dedicated item” that a dedication takes effect on offerings of the most sacred order and of lesser sanctity, which reads as a primary derivation. So they explain: according to Ulla he certainly must pay the value to Temple maintenance, as the mishna and Arakhin teach; “only the delay of the treasurers” means the Temple has nothing in the animal’s body except that the treasurers hold back its slaughter until it is appraised, and he owes the appraised value. The mishna is then no difficulty, since it says only that he owes a debt, not that the consecration takes effect on the body. The Gemara’s difficulty is rather this: since Ulla holds a burnt offering can be associated with the priests’ dedications, the dedication must take effect on the animal’s body. For a priest’s dedication is unlike Temple maintenance: “It is incumbent upon me to give a maneh to Temple maintenance” binds, since a statement to the Most High is like delivery to an ordinary person, but “It is incumbent upon me to give a maneh to the priests’ dedications” can be retracted, since a statement to an ordinary person is nothing; so it works only as “this object is a dedication,” on the object’s body. Then why only the treasurers’ delay, when slaughter is forbidden until redemption? The answer, “by rabbinic law”: by Torah law it does not take effect on the animal’s body at all; only by rabbinic law does it take effect on the body and forbid slaughter; and the verse’s main point is that it takes effect at least as a debt. Tosafot’s teacher also found in the name of the Ri: the question is from Ulla’s mentioning Temple maintenance and not the priests’ dedications, implying he holds like Rav Huna that the priests’ dedications are nothing, which contradicts his derivation that one can associate with them; and the answer is that his derivation from “every dedicated item” for the priests’ dedications is rabbinic. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a16.1: But didn’t Ulla say: one who associates a burnt offering for the value of Temple maintenance has only the delay of the treasurer alone. That is, nothing takes effect on it, and it requires neither any redemption nor any waiting, only the delay of the treasurer alone: that is, as soon as the treasurer of the Temple comes, he gives permission to slaughter it, and they slaughter it as a burnt offering at once, without redemption. And since the sanctity of Temple maintenance does not take effect on it, all the more so a dedication does not take effect on it. For Rav Huna, who holds that the consecration for Temple maintenance takes effect on it, says that they do not take effect for dedications to priests; all the more so Ulla, who says that it does not take effect for Temple maintenance, [must hold] a fortiori that they do not take effect for dedications either. And this is difficult for Ulla, who said “dedicated item, every dedicated item.”
gershom:a17.1: Ulla could say to you: yes, by Torah law a dedication does not take effect on them, since one who associates a burnt offering with Temple maintenance has only the treasurer’s delay; but I spoke by rabbinic law, that a dedication takes effect on them. And the verse that writes “every dedicated item” comes for misuse: that one is liable for misuse of dedications, from the inclusion of “every.”
rashi:b1.1: Treasurers: that it is not sacrificed until the treasurers come to stand over it, as we say elsewhere (Ta’anit 26a): How can a person’s offering be sacrificed while he does not stand over it? But he gives no monetary value to Temple maintenance, and all the more so not to dedications to priests, since even Rav Huna, who disagreed regarding dedications to priests, agreed regarding Temple maintenance.
rashi:b2.1: And it answers, by rabbinic law: that earlier baraita, which omitted items consecrated for the altar, meaning that a consecration of value takes effect on them, [means that] it takes effect by rabbinic law, since by Torah law there is only the treasurers’ delay. And Ulla too, when he answered it, answered it by rabbinic law, and the verse is a mere support; the main point of the verse comes for misuse, to include dedications to priests in misuse. And this is its implication: every dedication is the Lord’s, so that if one derived even slight benefit from it, he has misused.
rashi:b5.1: To include the portions of offerings of lesser sanctity in misuse: since it is written “the Lord’s.” From that [teaching] of Rabbi, Rabbi Yannai derives offerings of the most sacred order as well, since “all the fat” is written. And the reason Rabbi said “offerings of lesser sanctity” is that, in his view, the sin offering and guilt offering are evidently included in “the holy items of the Lord,” since the owners have nothing in them, and there was no need to include [their] sacrificial portions; but according to Rabbi Yannai, at any rate, they needed to be included, even though “whether the sin offering or the guilt offering, it is most holy” is written [in the portion] “Command Aaron.” Another version, [marked] Yerushalmi: “From where do we derive it?” That is, what indicates that this “every dedicated item” takes effect on items consecrated for the altar?
rashi:b5.2: Are they sacrificed: that is, if he associated them with Temple maintenance, why do we sacrifice them without redemption, as he says there is only the treasurers’ delay? But this verse written above, “every dedicated item is holy,” implies that a dedication takes effect on every single sacred item, and it is forbidden for slaughter and for sacrifice until it is redeemed for the Temple by a consecration of value. [This explains a question, “Are they sacrificed?”, that is not in our printed Gemara; Rabbeinu Gershom’s text has it too.]
tosafot:b3.1: For misuse (“most holy” is written): this is somewhat difficult. Since we do not interpret “every dedicated item” to say that it speaks of dedications to priests, then where is “most holy” written regarding dedications to priests? My teacher HaRaMaR says that it relies on another verse written regarding dedications to priests: “But the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy unto the Lord, as a field dedicated; the possession of it shall be the priest’s” (Leviticus 27:21); and “most holy” is not precise, but means “holy unto the Lord.” And my teacher says: even if it did not interpret “every” to include dedications to priests, he nevertheless knows that the plain meaning of the verse, “most holy,” refers to dedications to priests, since it is written after it, “shall be sold or redeemed,” and that means dedications to priests, which have no redemption, whereas dedications for Temple maintenance, on the contrary, stand entirely for redemption. Nevertheless, an extra word was needed to include the consecration of value, since “the field … holy unto the Lord” implies excluding them; but misuse we learn from its plain meaning.
gershom:b1.1: Why do I need a verse for misuse? “Most holy” is written. Evidently its law is like offerings of the most sacred order, for which one is liable for misuse.
gershom:b2.1: And according to your reasoning, that which Rabbi Yannai said: misuse is explicit only, etc. Another version: “But Rav Huna states a verse!” That one is needed for that which we learned, etc.
gershom:b3.1: And did Ulla say this? But didn’t Ulla say, etc. Evidently, items consecrated for the altar are not taken by items consecrated for Temple maintenance, and all the more so dedications do not take effect.
gershom:b4.1: And items consecrated for the altar that one associated with dedications to priests: are they sacrificed? (As he says: a burnt offering that one associated with items consecrated for Temple maintenance has only the treasurer’s delay, and all the more so dedications.) But Ulla states a verse, “every dedicated item is most holy,” teaching that it takes effect on every single sacred item! [Like Rashi’s (rashi:b5.2), Rabbeinu Gershom’s text has a question “are they sacrificed?” that is not in our printed Gemara.]
gershom:b5.1: Ulla could say to you: it is by rabbinic law that dedications take effect on items consecrated for the altar.
gershom:b6.1: And this verse, “every dedicated item,” does not come for this; rather, it is a mere support. Then what does the verse “every dedicated item” come for? “Every” is needed for misuse of dedications, etc.
tosafot:b7.1: The matter itself: [one who consecrates a burnt offering for Temple maintenance] has only the delay of the treasurers: that is, the treasurers’ appraisal, that they hold it back from slaughter until they appraise it; but they cannot hold back the slaughter until it is redeemed, since the consecration of value is only a debt, by the decree of the verse.
tosafot:b7.2: They raised an objection: [one who consecrates a burnt offering for Temple maintenance] is forbidden to slaughter it until it is redeemed: since the dedication takes hold on the body of the burnt offering. And it answers: it is by rabbinic law that slaughtering it is forbidden, but by Torah law he is certainly obligated to pay the value to Temple maintenance. And in the chapter Tevul Yom (Zevaḥim 103a) it says: it is not necessary [to say this] according to the one who says items consecrated for Temple maintenance [take effect] by Torah law; but even according to the one who says they do not take effect, that applies to the flesh. Now this is very difficult: is there anyone who says that items consecrated for Temple maintenance do not take effect by a consecration of value? And from this halakha Rashi settled it there, explaining that “according to the one who says they take effect” is from the question here, which seeks to prove that it is forbidden to slaughter it by Torah law, and “even according to the one who says they do not take effect” is from here, where it concludes that it is by rabbinic law; in any case, that applies to the flesh, but [the consecration] does take effect on the hide, and it requires redemption.
gershom:b7.1: A burnt offering that one associated with items consecrated for Temple maintenance is forbidden to slaughter until it is redeemed: as we said, if a vow, he gives their value, and if a gift-offering, he gives its benefit. What is “forbidden until it is redeemed”? By rabbinic law.
gershom:b8.1: And if he transgressed and slaughtered it without redemption, what he did is done.
rashi:b9.1: Two counts of misuse: one on account of items consecrated for the altar and one on account of items consecrated for Temple maintenance. And if it is by rabbinic law, the sanctity of Temple maintenance takes effect only by rabbinic law.
rashi:b9.2: Fit: had the latter sanctity been by Torah law; and it would be fit, were it not that his consecration [takes effect only by rabbinic law] and not by Torah law. [The printed wording of this comment is garbled.]
tosafot:b9.1: And if by rabbinic law, why two counts of misuse? And if you say: but we find in several places that one is liable for misuse by rabbinic law, regarding blood and the eggs of turtledoves (Me’ila 12)? One can say: that applies to something people do not keep away from, but here they already keep away from it on account of the first consecration.
gershom:b9.1: If so, say the latter clause: and one is liable for misuse of it, if he derived benefit from it or from its shearings, if he derived benefit from it.
gershom:b10.1: Two counts of misuse: one on account of items consecrated for the altar and one on account of items consecrated for Temple maintenance. And if it is forbidden by rabbinic law, why two counts of misuse? Say: it is fit for one to be liable for two counts of misuse in it, had it been forbidden by Torah law; but since it is by rabbinic law, there is only one misuse in it.
gershom:b11.1: And if they died: blemished ones, those of which it said, “both items consecrated for the altar,” etc.
rashi:b11.1: Both items consecrated for the altar, etc.: and this “if they died they must be buried” refers to all of them. Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis both derive their reasons from a verse below, both according to Rabbi Yoḥanan and according to Reish Lakish.
tosafot:b11.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: [according to the Rabbis,] both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included in standing and valuation: and the mishna’s “if they died they must be buried” refers also to the offerings of the most sacred order [i.e., the altar offerings] of the latter clause. And Rabbi Shimon disagrees and says that items consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included in standing and valuation].
gershom:b12.1: They must be buried. Rabbi Shimon says: items consecrated for Temple maintenance, if they died, can be redeemed. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: according to the Rabbis, who say “if they died they must be buried,” both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included in standing and valuation. Therefore, since they died and it is impossible to perform standing and valuation for them, they are not redeemed but buried.
tosafot:b12.1: And Reish Lakish said: [according to the Rabbis,] items consecrated for the altar were not, items consecrated for Temple maintenance were: and the mishna’s “if they died they must be buried” refers only to items consecrated for Temple maintenance. And even though it teaches at the start of the clause, “both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance, one may not alter them,” which implies that the whole mishna refers to both, this is not difficult, since necessarily not all of it refers [to both]: the consecration of value refers only to items consecrated for the altar. And Rabbi Shimon disagrees with the Rabbis and says that, on the contrary, the reverse is reasonable: items consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included], and items consecrated for the altar were; and these are lines of reasoning opposite to each other.
gershom:b13.1: And Reish Lakish said: according to the Rabbis, items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included in standing, and about them they say “if they died they must be buried.” And this one and that one agree, both Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish, that according to Rabbi Shimon items consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation [and] items consecrated for Temple maintenance were not, since Rabbi Shimon says explicitly that only items consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed. And everyone agrees, the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish, that one blemished from the outset, if it died, is redeemed, since it was not included in standing and valuation.
rashi:b13.1: This one and that one: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish agree that according to Rabbi Shimon items consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included], but items consecrated for the altar were, since it teaches “items consecrated for Temple maintenance can be redeemed” and does not say simply “can be redeemed”; by implication, he spoke specifically.
rashi:b13.2: And everyone agrees: and furthermore both agree that according to everyone, both Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, one blemished from the outset was not in [the halakha of] standing and valuation, with items consecrated for the altar, as the reason is explained below. And with items consecrated for Temple maintenance it does not speak of anything blemished from the outset, for they agree that according to the Rabbis items consecrated for Temple maintenance require standing and valuation, whether it became blemished after the consecration or its blemish preceded its consecration; for with items consecrated for Temple maintenance we do not distinguish between one blemished from the outset and an unblemished one that became blemished, since [that consecration] takes effect even on wood and stones.
tosafot:b13.1: And everyone agrees that one blemished from the outset was not [included]: and this is specifically with items consecrated for the altar; but with items consecrated for Temple maintenance, even according to the one who holds [they were included], there is no distinction between an unblemished one and one blemished from the outset; and so the whole passage proves.
rashi:b14.1: This is why Rabbi Shimon needed to explain: for had he said simply “can be redeemed,” since the first tanna spoke of both, it would have implied that he disputes regarding both; therefore he explained.
rashi:b15.1: But according to Reish Lakish: who said that the Rabbis refer only to items consecrated for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b15.2: Why must he: Rabbi Shimon explain?
rashi:b15.3: Let him say: simply, and I would know that he refers only to Temple maintenance, since regarding items consecrated for the altar [the first tanna] spoke above of nothing at all, neither of redemption nor of burial.
tosafot:b15.1: But according to Reish Lakish: who says that the Rabbis do not speak of items consecrated for the altar at all, since they were not included in standing [and valuation], and if they died they [should] be redeemed. It is somewhat difficult: from where does he know this? Perhaps it speaks of items consecrated for the altar, and the reason is that one does not redeem consecrated animals to feed them to the dogs.
gershom:b14.1: But according to Reish Lakish, who said that according to the Rabbis items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included and about them they say “they must be buried,” why must Rabbi Shimon explain, “items consecrated for Temple maintenance, if they died, can be redeemed”? Let him say “if they died they can be redeemed,” and we would know that Rabbi Shimon is responding to what the Rabbis said.
rashi:b16.1: Rabbi Shimon: of the mishna did not know what the Rabbis were saying, and thought that the Rabbis refer to both.
gershom:b15.1: Reish Lakish could say to you: Rabbi Shimon did not know about what the Rabbis said “they must be buried,” and this is what he says to them: if regarding items consecrated for the altar we learned “if they died they must be buried,” etc. It is taught in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan, as he says that according to the Rabbis both this and that were included in standing and valuation: “And if it be any non-kosher animal,” etc., “then he shall set the animal before the priest,” which requires standing and valuation both for items consecrated for the altar and for items consecrated for Temple maintenance. For the permanently blemished ones are items consecrated for the altar, and the actual non-kosher animal is items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which is consecrated only for its value; and standing and valuation is written regarding both.
gershom:b16.1: Another version: “from the fact that it teaches,” and all of it as in the first version.
